title: Making Decisions Checkpoint
intro: Your programs can now take different paths: if, else, chains, nesting, switch and the ternary. Twelve rounds, one from every idea in this module. First-try answers earn three stars!

rounds.prompt: What must go inside the round brackets of an `if`?
options: Something that produces true or false
Any number, where 0 counts as false
The instruction you want to run
rounds.explain: Java insists on a boolean. A comparison, a logical expression, or a boolean variable all work; `if (score)` with an int is a compile error.

rounds.prompt: The score is only 10. What does this print?
rounds.explain: The semicolon ends the `if` immediately, so it guards an empty instruction. The block below is then just an ordinary block, and it always runs.

rounds.prompt: This congratulates a score of 20. What is missing?
options: Braces: without them only the first instruction belongs to the if
An else before the second print
rounds.explain: Java ignores indentation. Only one instruction attaches to a braceless `if`, so the second print always runs.

rounds.prompt: Marks are 80. How many lines does this print?
rounds.explain: A chain stops at the first true test. 80 is also 60 or more, but Java never reaches that test once B has matched.

rounds.prompt: Top marks of 95 come out as a D. What is wrong?
options: The loosest test is first, so nothing below it can ever run
The chain needs a final else
rounds.explain: Every mark of 40 or more matches the first test. Range tests have to be ordered from narrowest to widest.

rounds.prompt: Why does removing the final `else` sometimes cause `variable might not have been initialized`?
options: Java cannot prove that every path gives the variable a value
Every chain must end with else
The variable should have been final
rounds.explain: Without a catch-all there is a route through the code where nothing is assigned, and Java refuses to let you read a local variable that might hold nothing.

rounds.prompt: Both conditions must be true and there is nothing to do in between. Which is better?
rounds.explain: `&&` gives one condition and one level of indentation. Nesting is for when each branch needs to do something different.

rounds.prompt: There is no break after case 1. What does this print?
rounds.explain: This is fall-through: Java runs the matching case and keeps going downwards until it meets a `break`.

rounds.prompt: Which of these can a switch NOT match?
rounds.explain: A switch compares one value against fixed known values. Ranges and comparisons belong in an `else if` chain.

rounds.prompt: Age is 30. What does this store in price?
rounds.explain: The condition is false, so the ternary chooses the value after the colon. Read it as: condition ? whenTrue : whenFalse.

rounds.prompt: Match each tool to the job it fits best.

pairs.right: Do something only when a condition holds
The path taken when the if was false
A detail that applies inside one branch
Match one value against fixed options
Choose between two values in one line

rounds.explain: Six tools, six shapes of decision. Choosing the one that fits is most of what makes code readable.

rounds.prompt: Build a grade chain that works: highest band first, then the rest, ending with a catch-all.
rounds.explain: The narrowest test has to come first, because the chain stops at the first true condition. The closing `else` catches everything left and guarantees `grade` is always given a value.
